options: CH₃O⁻
CH₃CO₂⁻
CH₃CH₂⁻
NH₂⁻

feedback.hint: Look for equivalent or near-equivalent atoms that can share charge through π bonding.
feedback.solution: The acetate ion delocalizes negative charge over two oxygen atoms. The other listed anions lack comparable resonance stabilization.

questions.prompt: A tertiary alkyl halide in water undergoes substitution. Which pathway is generally more plausible?
options: SN2, because the tertiary center is unhindered
SN1, because ionization can form a stabilized carbocation
Neither pathway can occur in a protic solvent
A radical chain is required

feedback.hint: Tertiary substitution centers are strongly sterically hindered for backside attack.
feedback.solution: SN1 is generally favored for a tertiary center in a polar protic solvent because carbocation formation is stabilized and SN2 is sterically hindered. The actual pathway depends on the full substrate and conditions.

questions.prompt: Which geometric arrangement is required for a typical concerted E2 elimination?
options: Anti-periplanar C–H and C–leaving-group bonds
Any arrangement because the carbocation rotates
A tetrahedral carbon with no beta hydrogen
An aromatic ring with all sigma bonds fixed

feedback.hint: E2 forms the π bond as the C–H and C–leaving-group bonds break together.
feedback.solution: The required orbital alignment is usually anti-periplanar; in a cyclohexane chair this is trans-diaxial.

modifications: Clarified the typical E2 answer option as anti-periplanar; atypical syn elimination is not presented as equally typical.

questions.prompt: Why are acid chlorides generally more reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution than amides?
options: Chloride is a better leaving group and donates less by resonance
Amide carbonyl carbon is more electrophilic
Amides have no carbonyl resonance
Chloride prevents nucleophilic attack

feedback.hint: Compare leaving-group basicity and resonance donation into the carbonyl.
feedback.solution: Chloride is a weaker base and better leaving group than an amide anion, while nitrogen donates strongly by resonance and reduces amide carbonyl electrophilicity.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the carboxylate ion's resonance structures is correct?
options: Only electrons move between the structures; the real ion is a hybrid with two equivalent C–O bonds of intermediate length.
The ion flips rapidly between two different molecules.
Each structure is an isolated species present in solution.
Atoms move to new positions between structures.

feedback.hint: Recall what resonance does and does not describe.
feedback.solution: Resonance structures differ only in electron placement with the same atom positions and valences. The actual ion is a single delocalized hybrid, so both C–O bonds are equivalent with bond order about 1.5.

questions.prompt: A chiral secondary alkyl bromide reacts with cyanide by a concerted backside attack. What are the stereochemical and rate consequences?
options: Retention of configuration with a rate that depends on substrate only.
Loss of stereochemistry and a zero-order rate.
Racemization with a first-order rate in substrate.
Inversion of configuration at carbon, with a rate that depends on both the substrate and the nucleophile concentration.

feedback.hint: Backside attack in one step gives a specific geometric outcome and a bimolecular rate.
feedback.solution: A concerted SN2 step inverts the carbon center, and because both reactants are in the one rate-determining step the rate is second order overall: rate = k[RBr][CN⁻].

questions.prompt: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-methyl-2-butanol through a carbocation intermediate gives mainly which alkene, assuming Zaitsev selectivity?
options: 2-methyl-1-butene as the major product.
2-methyl-2-butene, the more substituted alkene.
No alkene forms.
3-methyl-1-butene as the major product.

feedback.hint: The more substituted alkene is usually more stable.
feedback.solution: Loss of a proton from the carbon that leads to the more substituted double bond gives 2-methyl-2-butene as the major product under thermodynamic (Zaitsev) control. The assumption can fail with bulky bases or when other pathways compete.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly states the reaction type?
options: A Grignard reagent with a ketone undergoes nucleophilic addition; an amine with an acid chloride undergoes nucleophilic acyl substitution.
Both are electrophilic aromatic substitutions.
A Grignard reagent with a ketone is an acyl substitution; an amine with an acid chloride is an addition.
Both are eliminations.

feedback.hint: Look for a leaving group on the carbonyl carbon.
feedback.solution: Ketones lack a good leaving group, so a nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated. Acid chlorides have a good leaving group (chloride), so the addition intermediate collapses and expels it, giving net substitution.

questions.prompt: Which ordering of reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution is correct?
options: Amide > ester > thioester, because nitrogen is the most electronegative.
Thioester > ester > amide, because sulfur donates less resonance stabilization to the carbonyl than oxygen, and nitrogen donates the most.
All three react at the same rate.
Ester > thioester > amide, because oxygen is a better leaving group than sulfur.

feedback.hint: Consider resonance donation into the carbonyl and leaving-group basicity.
feedback.solution: Nitrogen's strong resonance donation stabilizes amides; sulfur's poor 3p–2p overlap gives thioesters little stabilization and a weaker-base leaving group. Hence acetyl-CoA is an activated acyl donor while peptide bonds persist.

Independent structural evidence and a calibrated material balance.

feedback.hint: Group by sample and average both supplied reporting channels.
feedback.solution: Each group has three balanced reports; raw means retain reporting offset and channel gain.

questions.prompt: Both channels in the independent blank have true amount zero. What peak A additive reporting offset in arbitrary area units follows from its CSV mean? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Use the blank mean; do not call its area material amount.
feedback.solution: Blank mean area A is 3.0 units, identifying its stipulated additive offset.

questions.prompt: Independent std_a contains 10.0 µmol A and no B. After subtracting the blank A area from its mean, what peak A gain in area units per µmol follows? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide blank-corrected pure-standard area by its known amount.
feedback.solution: (23−3)/10=2 area units per µmol. This is a synthetic reporting gain, not an intrinsic enantiomer absorptivity difference.

questions.prompt: Calibrate both channels using their separate 10.0 µmol standards and blank. What signed A enantiomeric excess, 100(n_A−n_B)/(n_A+n_B), in percent follows for mix_2? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Convert blank-corrected areas to amounts with each channel gain before normalizing.
feedback.solution: Amounts are A=7 and B=3 µmol, giving signed A excess 40%. Area-only excess is different.

questions.prompt: Using the same two standards and blank, what calibrated amount ratio n_B/n_A follows for mix_4? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Use each channel calibration independently; retain the stated B/A order.

questions.prompt: Select conclusions supported by the supplied identities and calibration.

options: The stipulated additive reporting offset in each channel.
Every possible coeluting compound in any real sample.
A nonzero amount of both enantiomers.

response_fields.prompt: What do unequal gains mean in this construction?
options: Peak-specific reporting/recovery factors, not a claimed intrinsic UV absorption difference in an achiral environment.
All enantiomers have different intrinsic UV absorption in the same achiral environment.
Raw area is already amount regardless of calibration.

response_fields.prompt: The standards independently identify A as positive and B as negative optical enantiomers under matched conditions. What can be inferred about R/S here?
options: No absolute descriptor from optical sign or retention order alone.
Positive A must be R.
The larger peak must be S.

evidence: A zero-amount reference identifies its reporting baseline under the declared model.
The model explicitly assigns observation-channel gains.
Optical sign and retention identity do not supply an absolute configuration.

feedback.hint: Keep reporting calibration, peak identity and absolute configuration separate.
feedback.solution: The supplied blank and pure standards constrain the linear reporting model. Optical identities are independently given; no R/S assignment follows.

questions.prompt: Which statements respect the synthetic reports? Select all that apply.
options: The three offsets deliberately balance around each constructed mean.
A chromatographic peak alone proves complete molecular purity.
Each channel needs its own standard factor before amount comparison.
Three repeats prove independent Gaussian instrument errors.
Mix_3 has equal calibrated A/B amounts despite unequal blank-corrected areas.

feedback.hint: Separate constructed response and amounts from real instrument or purity claims.
feedback.solution: Balanced reports, separately calibrated gains and the equal-amount mix_3 are supported. Noise independence and complete purity are not established.

questions.prompt: For mix_3, what does the declared two-enantiomer model establish after calibration?
options: A excess must remain because every larger peak means more molecules.
A meso compound is created by mixing enantiomers.
Equal A and B amounts and zero excess; raw area inequality reflects the assigned gains.

feedback.hint: Use calibrated amounts and distinguish a mixture from an internally achiral molecule.
feedback.solution: The calibrated amounts are 5 and 5 µmol. A racemic pair differs from a meso molecule; the response model does not prove real sample purity.

questions.prompt: How many π electrons are in benzene's conjugated ring? Enter the count.

feedback.hint: Count one electron from each of the six p orbitals.
feedback.solution: The six p orbitals contribute six π electrons, satisfying 4n+2 for n=1.

questions.prompt: How many π electrons are in the planar conjugated cyclobutadiene ring? Enter the count.

feedback.hint: Count the two π bonds in the cyclic system.
feedback.solution: Two π bonds contribute four electrons, a 4n count for n=1. A planar, continuously conjugated four-electron ring is antiaromatic.

questions.prompt: How many π electrons are in the cyclopentadienyl anion's conjugated ring? Enter the count.

feedback.hint: Include the lone pair in the p orbital as well as the two π bonds.
feedback.solution: Two π bonds contribute four electrons and the anionic p-orbital lone pair contributes two, for six total.

questions.prompt: How many π electrons are in the tropylium cation's conjugated ring? Enter the count.

feedback.hint: Count the three π bonds; the positive charge corresponds to an empty p orbital.
feedback.solution: Three π bonds contribute six π electrons. The planar, continuously conjugated ring satisfies 4n+2 for n=1.

questions.prompt: Which description gives the full aromaticity test used in this lesson?
options: Any cyclic molecule with an even number of atoms
A planar, cyclic, continuously conjugated π system with 4n+2 π electrons
Any ring with alternating single and double bonds in one drawing
Any conjugated ring with 4n π electrons

feedback.hint: Geometry and continuous p-orbital overlap matter as well as the electron count.
feedback.solution: Aromaticity requires a cyclic, planar, continuously conjugated system and a 4n+2 π-electron count.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes electrophilic aromatic substitution?
options: Electrophile adds to the ring to form a σ complex; loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity
The ring loses its substituent first, then the electrophile fills the vacancy
The electrophile replaces a carbon atom in the ring
The ring stays fully aromatic during bond formation and deprotonation

feedback.hint: Track the carbon that forms the new bond to E.
feedback.solution: The π system attacks E⁺, temporarily losing aromaticity in a σ complex. Deprotonation at the same carbon restores the aromatic ring.

questions.prompt: A methoxy group is attached at position 1 of benzene. Where does its resonance donation broadly favor a second EAS?
options: Meta only
Ortho and para
It does not affect orientation
It replaces the carbon bearing methoxy

feedback.hint: A lone pair on oxygen can donate into the ring.
feedback.solution: Methoxy donates by resonance and stabilizes ortho/para σ-complex contributors. This predicts broad positions, not a quantitative product ratio.

questions.prompt: Why does a nitro group broadly direct electrophilic aromatic substitution to the meta position?
options: Nitro donates a lone pair into the ring
The ortho/para σ-complex contributors place positive charge unfavorably relative to the withdrawing group
The meta carbon has no hydrogen
The nitro group prevents all resonance

feedback.hint: Compare the positive-charge locations in the σ-complex resonance contributors.
feedback.solution: Nitro withdraws electron density. The ortho and para pathways have especially unfavorable contributors with positive charge adjacent to the attached withdrawing group; the meta path avoids that contributor.

questions.prompt: A halogen on benzene generally deactivates the ring yet directs a second EAS ortho/para. Which explanation accounts for both effects?
options: Halogens donate only by induction
Inductive withdrawal deactivates; lone-pair resonance donation favors ortho/para σ complexes
Halogens make all ring positions equally reactive
The halogen leaves before the electrophile adds in every EAS

feedback.hint: Separate the inductive effect on rate from resonance effects on orientation.
feedback.solution: Halogens withdraw inductively and slow EAS overall, while lone-pair donation by resonance stabilizes ortho/para σ-complex contributors.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of an activated aryl chloride by methoxide?
options: Methoxide adds to the carbon bearing Cl, forming an anionic σ complex; loss of Cl⁻ restores aromaticity
Methoxide attacks from behind the C–Cl bond and displaces Cl⁻ in one concerted step
Cl⁻ leaves first to give an aryl cation, which methoxide then captures
Methoxide adds to the ring, and loss of H⁺ from the same carbon restores aromaticity

feedback.hint: Ask which atom bonds first and which group finally leaves the ipso carbon.
feedback.solution: The nucleophile adds to the ipso carbon, which becomes sp³ in a negatively charged Meisenheimer complex. The halide then leaves from that carbon, restoring the aromatic ring. Backside SN2 is blocked by the ring, an aryl cation is not stabilized by the π system, and losing H⁺ is the EAS pattern.

questions.prompt: Which aryl chloride is predicted to react fastest with methoxide by the SNAr addition–elimination mechanism?
options: Chlorobenzene
1-Chloro-3-nitrobenzene
1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene
1-Chloro-4-methoxybenzene

feedback.hint: Find the substituent that can hold the Meisenheimer complex's negative charge on its own atoms.
feedback.solution: The Meisenheimer charge sits ortho and para to the ipso carbon. A para nitro group can delocalize it onto oxygen. A meta nitro group gives only weaker inductive help, chlorobenzene has no activating group, and methoxy donates electron density, which destabilizes the anion.

questions.prompt: An activated aryl fluoride commonly undergoes SNAr faster than the corresponding aryl chloride, although the C–F bond is stronger. Which explanation fits the mechanism?
options: Fluoride is the best leaving group in SN2 reactions as well
Addition is usually rate-determining; fluorine's electronegativity makes the ipso carbon more electrophilic and stabilizes the anion, and C–F breaks only after the slow step
Fluorine donates a lone pair that makes the ring more nucleophilic
The C–F bond breaks before the nucleophile arrives

feedback.hint: Identify which step is slow and whether the carbon–halogen bond breaks in it.
feedback.solution: For activated rings the nucleophile's addition is usually rate-limiting. Fluorine's strong inductive withdrawal speeds that addition; C–F cleavage occurs in the faster elimination step. This is a qualitative trend, not a fixed rate ratio.

questions.prompt: A nitro group deactivates a ring toward EAS but activates it toward SNAr when it is ortho or para to the leaving group. What reconciles these roles?
options: Nitro donates electrons in SNAr and withdraws them in EAS
Withdrawing electron density destabilizes the cationic EAS σ complex but stabilizes the anionic SNAr σ complex
Nitro is the leaving group in SNAr
Both reactions proceed through the same cationic intermediate

feedback.hint: Compare the charge of the σ complex in each mechanism.
feedback.solution: The same electron-withdrawing group is unfavorable next to a positive charge (EAS) and favorable next to a negative charge it can delocalize onto its oxygens (SNAr). Its effect depends on the intermediate, not on a fixed activating label.

questions.prompt: When methoxide adds to C1 of 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, how many ring carbons carry the negative charge in at least one ring resonance contributor of the Meisenheimer complex? Do not count contributors that place the charge on nitro oxygens. Enter the count.

feedback.hint: The charge moves through the ring's remaining π bonds; label each carbon relative to the ipso carbon.
feedback.solution: The ring contributors place the charge on C2, C4 and C6, the carbons ortho and para to the ipso carbon, never on C3 or C5. That gives three carbons.

questions.prompt: In 1-chloro-3,5-dinitrobenzene, how many nitro groups are ortho or para to the carbon bearing chlorine? Enter the count.

feedback.hint: Number the ring from the C–Cl carbon as C1 and classify positions 3 and 5.
feedback.solution: Positions 3 and 5 are both meta to C1. Neither nitro group can accept the Meisenheimer charge by resonance, so the count is zero and the ring is far less activated than the 2,4-isomer.

questions.prompt: A neutral 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene molecule adds one methoxide ion to form a Meisenheimer complex. What is the complex's net charge? Enter a signed integer.

feedback.hint: Add the charges of the two species that combine in the addition step.
feedback.solution: Neutral substrate (0) plus methoxide (−1) gives a complex with net charge −1. Loss of Cl⁻ in the next step returns a neutral aromatic product.

questions.prompt: How many degrees of unsaturation does propene, C₃H₆, have? Enter the count.

feedback.hint: Use (2C + 2 − H − X)/2 for a neutral formula.
feedback.solution: (2×3 + 2 − 6)/2 = 1; the alkene has one degree of unsaturation.

questions.prompt: How many degrees of unsaturation does C₃H₇Br have? Count halogen like hydrogen.

feedback.hint: A halogen replaces one hydrogen in the formula relation.
feedback.solution: (2×3 + 2 − 7 − 1)/2 = 0; the saturated alkyl bromide has no rings or π bonds.

questions.prompt: Under a 1:1 addition model, how many mmol of HX are consumed by complete reaction of 0.35 mmol alkene?

feedback.hint: One alkene π bond accepts one HX equivalent in this model.
feedback.solution: The stipulated 1:1 mole ratio gives 0.35 mmol HX.

questions.prompt: A 1:1 alkene/Br₂ model starts with 1.20 mmol alkene and 0.90 mmol Br₂. What is the maximum mmol of addition product?

feedback.hint: The smaller reactant amount limits a 1:1 reaction.
feedback.solution: Br₂ is limiting, so the maximum product amount is 0.90 mmol under the stated model.

questions.prompt: In the usual carbocation model, which is the major constitutional product of acid-catalyzed hydration of 1-butene?
options: 1-butanol
2-butanol
Butane
Butanal

feedback.hint: Markovnikov orientation places OH on the more substituted alkene carbon.
feedback.solution: The standard acid-hydration model predicts 2-butanol; it does not by itself specify an exact stereoisomer ratio.

questions.prompt: In the standard model for Br₂ addition to cyclohexene, what relative stereochemical relationship is expected for the two bromines?
options: Cis, from syn attack on a free carbocation
Trans, from anti opening of a bromonium ion
No relative relationship can be predicted because the product is an alkane
Both bromines attach to the same carbon

feedback.hint: The bridged bromonium ion is opened from the opposite face.
feedback.solution: Anti addition to cyclohexene gives the trans 1,2-dibromide in the ideal introductory model.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes hydroboration–oxidation of 1-butene in the standard model?
options: It gives mainly 2-butanol by anti addition through a free carbocation.
It gives mainly 1-butanol by syn, non-Markovnikov hydration without a carbocation intermediate.
It gives butane by adding hydrogen twice.
It gives a vicinal dibromide.

feedback.hint: Track which carbon receives boron in the concerted addition, then the group that replaces it.
feedback.solution: Boron attaches to the less substituted carbon with syn addition; oxidation replaces C–B with C–OH, giving 1-butanol.

questions.prompt: Which statements match the standard introductory models? Select all that apply.
options: Hydrohalogenation may form a carbocation and can permit rearrangement.
Halogenation uses a bridged halonium intermediate and gives anti addition.
Hydroboration–oxidation gives a syn, non-Markovnikov hydration outcome.
Markovnikov regiochemistry alone determines whether addition is syn or anti.

feedback.hint: Separate carbon placement (regiochemistry) from the relative faces of bond formation (stereochemistry).
feedback.solution: The first three statements describe the selected models. Markovnikov specifies orientation across the double bond, not syn/anti stereochemistry.

questions.prompt: What does “Markovnikov orientation” specify for an unsymmetrical alkene addition?
options: Which carbon receives each of the two added groups, under the stated model
Whether the two groups add from the same or opposite faces
The absolute R/S configuration of every product
The percentage yield of the reaction

feedback.hint: The term describes regioselectivity.
feedback.solution: Markovnikov orientation is a regiochemical description; stereochemistry, configuration and yield require separate information.

questions.prompt: How many degrees of unsaturation are in propyne, C₃H₄?

feedback.solution: (2×3 + 2 − 4)/2 = 2, corresponding to the two π-bond equivalents of a triple bond.

questions.prompt: After adding one equivalent of H₂ to one alkyne triple bond, how many π bonds remain in the product?

feedback.hint: One of the two π bonds is removed.
feedback.solution: One π bond remains as the alkene product.

questions.prompt: A 1:2 alkyne/H₂ model fully reduces 0.42 mmol alkyne. How many mmol of H₂ are consumed?

feedback.hint: Complete reduction uses two H₂ equivalents per triple bond.
feedback.solution: 0.42×2 = 0.84 mmol H₂ under the stated complete-reduction model.

questions.prompt: Complete addition of two H₂ equivalents to C₄H₆ gives the saturated four-carbon alkane. How many hydrogen atoms are in its formula?

feedback.hint: Add four hydrogen atoms while retaining all four carbons.
feedback.solution: C₄H₆ + 2 H₂ gives C₄H₁₀, so the hydrogen subscript is 10.

questions.prompt: What is the predicted carbonyl product of standard Markovnikov hydration of propyne after enol tautomerization?
options: Propanal
Acetone (propanone)
Propene
Propanol

feedback.hint: Place OH on the more substituted carbon in the enol, then tautomerize.
feedback.solution: The enol CH₃C(OH)=CH₂ tautomerizes to acetone.

questions.prompt: What carbonyl product is predicted when terminal propyne undergoes the standard bulky-borane hydroboration–oxidation model?
options: Acetone, from Markovnikov enol formation
Propanal, from non-Markovnikov enol formation and tautomerization
Propane, from complete reduction
Propanol, from reduction of the carbonyl

feedback.hint: The terminal-alkyne route places oxygen at the terminal carbon before tautomerization.
feedback.solution: The hydroboration route gives a terminal enol that tautomerizes to propanal in the standard model.

questions.prompt: Which pairing gives the usual partial-reduction outcomes for 2-butyne?
options: Lindlar model → cis-2-butene; dissolving-metal model → trans-2-butene
Lindlar model → trans-2-butene; dissolving-metal model → cis-2-butene
Both models → butane
Both models → 2-butanone

feedback.hint: The two partial reductions deliver hydrogen with different relative stereochemical outcomes.
feedback.solution: The Lindlar model gives syn reduction to the cis alkene; the dissolving-metal model gives the trans alkene.

questions.prompt: Which statements are supported by the selected alkyne models? Select all that apply.
options: Complete reduction uses two H₂ equivalents per triple bond and gives an alkane.
The standard Lindlar partial reduction stops at a cis alkene.
Hydroboration–oxidation of a terminal alkyne can give an aldehyde after tautomerization.
Enol-to-carbonyl tautomerization removes one molecule of water.

feedback.hint: Check the carbon/hydrogen ledger and distinguish the hydration and reduction pathways.
feedback.solution: The first three statements match the selected models. Tautomerization relocates a proton and π bond while conserving atoms; it is not dehydration.

questions.prompt: What changes in enol-to-carbonyl tautomerization?
options: A proton and a π bond change position while the molecular formula is conserved.
The molecule loses CO₂.
The triple bond is reduced to an alkane.
A water molecule is eliminated in every case.

feedback.hint: Compare the enol and carbonyl formulas and locate the proton.
feedback.solution: Tautomerization is an atom-conserving proton and double-bond rearrangement.
